description: Imleria badia, the Bay Bolete, is a pored mushroom of conifer and mixed woodland, long known under the name Boletus badius before being moved to the genus Imleria. It has a chestnut to bay-brown cap that is finely velvety or suede-like when dry and somewhat sticky when wet, growing roughly 4-15 cm across. The underside bears pores (tubes), not gills, which are cream to pale yellow and bruise blue-green to dull bluish on touch or with age. The stipe is paler brown, fibrous and often streaky, without a ring and without a coarse net. It is a popular, good edible when thoroughly cooked, with a mild nutty flavour, but should never be eaten raw. The main confusion species to rule out is the bitter Tylopilus felleus, which has pinkish pores and an intensely bitter taste; always confirm pores rather than gills and check for the characteristic blue-green bruising.
edibilityNotes: A well-regarded edible bolete that must be cooked before eating; raw boletes can cause gastrointestinal upset. The bluing reaction of the pores is normal for this species and not a sign of toxicity. As with all foraged fungi, eat only after a confident identification and try a small portion first. Like many wild mushrooms it can accumulate heavy metals and radiocaesium, so avoid harvesting from contaminated or roadside sites and eat in moderation.
distribution: Widespread across Europe and present in North America; reported more broadly across temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Tylopilus felleus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Bitter bolete; pores are whitish then pinkish (not yellow and not bruising blue-green), stipe bears a coarse dark net, and the flesh is intensely bitter, making it inedible. A bitter taste test on a tiny piece readily separates it. Not deadly but will ruin a dish.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Boletus / Imleria species with red pores
dangerousLookalikes.note: Bay Bolete always has cream-to-yellow pores. Any bolete with orange-to-red pore mouths (e.g. Suillellus / Rubroboletus group) should be left alone unless separately confirmed, as several red-pored, blue-staining boletes are toxic raw or outright poisonous.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hortiboletus / Xerocomellus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several smaller brown, blue-bruising boletes in the Xerocomus group resemble young Bay Bolete. They are not dangerous but are easily confused; the Bay Bolete is distinguished by its larger size, tacky cap when wet, and prompt blue-green bruising of cream-yellow pores.
